utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I won't ask Madam Registrar to call the case since she has a very bad throat. And welcome back, Ms. Fleming, and Happy New Year to you. Before we start, we have several questions about that third autopsy report. Yesterday, we go through all the transcript, and we found very few bases for we have to accept those autopsy report. The only place we found is on the page 4.414, during the examination by Mr. Scott to Witness CC. The question asked is like this: "Did you hear around the time that a prisoner at Dobrkovici school had been killed or did someone tell you that? " We believe that it is hearsay evidence, and that foundation is not that sound. Another thing, that the name "Krilic" is mentioned, but I don't know which Krilic it is. I hope the Prosecutor could provide us with more information in this direction so that we could make the proper decisions in this respect. This morning, we will go with this witness with the other two reports. And during the break, no matter at 11.00 or during the lunch break, we hope the Prosecutor could do some research in this aspect. Otherwise, we'll refuse to accept that autopsy report because this has to be based on a sound foundation, and there has to be a close connection with the incidents charged in the indictment. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And yes, I will consult with my colleagues on the team. And if there's any additional information that we can provide in respect of the Krilic matter, we will do so. I did want to add very briefly, if -- and to perhaps suggest that I may have misunderstood, yesterday at least, the status in respect of this report because it had been submitted and accepted by the Trial Chamber and already -- it had been my understanding, already admitted into evidence pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision. In the decision, the Trial Chamber had found that the statements of the expert as contained in the report were relevant, and so -- it was my impression, I guess, that the Trial Chamber had already made some type of finding in respect to the relevance and the admissibility of the report; that's not to say, as Judge Clark suggested yesterday, that the Trial Chamber can't consider relevancy or even reconsider relevancy at any time during the proceedings. So I think all of us agree that this is not central to the charges in this case. The Prosecutor continues to assert that the evidence is relevant, but it's certainly not central, and we will consult during the next break and we will provide the Trial Chamber with any additional information. Or, if in fact there is nothing more to add than what the Trial Chamber found in its search of the record, then we may very well propose to just move forward without testimony on that particular report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could Mr. Usher bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please remember that you are still under the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, good morning.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When we had reached the end of proceedings yesterday, you had just finished describing injuries to the body that was subsequently identified as that of Nenad Harmandic, particularly injuries to the shoulder blade and clavicle of Mr. Harmandic. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You had also mentioned a fracture of he lower jawbone of Mr. Harmandic, and I wanted to ask you if you could describe that particular injury in greater detail as well as whatever light you can shed on how -- the features of that injury and how it relates to the other injuries which you found on this body.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the autopsy, we found a fracture of the lower jaw between the teeth number 3 and 4. It was an isolated fracture of the lower jaw on the left-hand side. And such injury would have been consistent with a swing, with having been sustained by a swing of a blunt mechanical instrument.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And finally, Dr. Zujo, yesterday you mentioned, I believe, an injury to the left cheekbone, and also I understand from your report that the injury to the cheekbone is -- or perhaps you found to be related to additional injuries and damage to the upper jaw of Nenad Harmandic; and I would ask you at this time to describe and inform the Trial Chamber your findings in respect of those injuries to the cheekbone and upper jaw.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the left cheekbone is concerned, during the autopsy, we found a part of it missing. It was round in shape, which led us to believe that it could have been caused by a bullet fired from a firearm. And also, the state of the upper jaw, we were unable to determine the state of teeth because of the heavy damage, which meant that the projectile must have affected the upper jaw, causing multiple fractures in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During the course of the autopsy, were you able to locate or to find the bullet which caused this particular injury?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an injury in which the bullet went through the body and exited, so we did not find the bullet with the remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Zujo, you have described for us a variety of injuries found in the body of Nenad Harmandic. In the report that you submitted to the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 10 on page 6, you described a number of these injuries, primarily the fractures, as being caused by a combination of multiple blows from a blunt object. You described these as non-specific injuries. You then went on in paragraph 10 to characterise the injury to the left cheekbone caused by a bullet entry as being the specific cause of death. And I wanted to ask you if you could just elaborate on that for us just a little bit, the non-specific injuries versus the specific cause of death.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the injuries on the bones themselves are concerned, the injuries to the left shoulder blade, the collarbone, the pelvic bones, the right ulna and fibula, they were all inflicted with blunt mechanical object and they are all non-specific in character; whereas, the specific injury was the one in the left cheek bone which was caused by a bullet from a firearm. And in the conclusion which we reached, we established that the cause of death was due to the head injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, were you able to make any findings in respect of the timing; that is to say, whether the non-specific injuries that you've described occurred before or possibly after the specific injury which resulted in the death of Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the order of injuries is concerned, I am unable to make any determination. However, all the injuries which we found during the autopsy were injuries sustained while the person was alive and I cannot say more about the actual time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, finally, in your statement submitted to the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 11, you stated that, in summary, Nenad Harmandic was first severely beaten and then shot to death. Does that remain your finding today as to the death of Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I saying that the actual cause of death was what I have stated, and that all those injuries were inflicted while the victim was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Zujo, now I would like to move on to the second of the autopsy reports that is a part of your statement to the Trial Chamber, which relates to your -- the exhumation -- I'm sorry, let me back up. I'm not at all finished with the first of these. I need to ask you additional questions about Nenad Harmandic, particularly if you could inform the Trial Chamber how the body which you examined in the autopsy was subsequently identified as that of Nenad Harmandic. And perhaps I could ask you to inform us if there are general procedures or practices that apply in these situations, and then to bring that down to specific factors which led to the conclusion, in this case, that this particular body was that of Nenad Harmandic.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we start the autopsy, we establish contact with the next of kin, and we receive from the next of kin certain information which will help us in the process of identification, such as what he was wearing before he died, then the height, the age, the state of teeth, whether he had any wounds or injuries of the bones which he had sustained previously, so that we could -- so that we could focus on that during the autopsy, finding certain scar tissue. After we start the autopsy, we first conduct a full description of the body; that is, all the clothing found on the remains, including colours and textures. Then the length of the remains, such as the skeletal remains, and then the length of the femur. And on the basis of that, we established the height of the victim, then the age of the victim based on certain bones in the skull. Then we determine the sex of the victim, and then look for more specific scar tissue, if there is such a thing. Then we photograph all the items in detail and -- because in this case, we only had skeletal remains, so we could not conduct a dactyloscopy, we contact the family, and compare what the family had told us and all the items that we have found. And only after we have conducted this comparison, we let family members come in for the direct identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, then, in reference to some of the more general physical characteristics of this skeletonised body which you examined, in terms of size, age, et cetera, did you find those characteristics to be consistent with information that you had received from members of the Harmandic family?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found that the height of the body was 182 to 183 centimetres; however, we had other parameters that we had and compared with the actual height of 182, 183 centimetres, and we concluded that we could add 2 to 5 centimetres as a margin of error, and that is a standard one in the literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, in your report, you make reference to a specific factor, that is, a prior bullet wound, self-inflicted bullet wound to the left thigh, in which a 6.35 millimetre, I believe, bullet had been lodged in the left leg of Mr. Harmandic. Was that a factor in the identification of this body?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the autopsy, we found a bullet, 6.35 millimetre, in the thigh -- left thighbone area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right thighbone area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right thighbone. Apologise. Was this finding consistent with information that had been provided by the family about a previously -- a previous injury to Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received this information that he had this injury in the right thighbone -- thigh area, and this also information was consistent with our own findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And finally, as indicated in your report, a final identification was made by the son of Nenad Harmandic. He viewed the body and was able to make a positive identification. Could I ask you to tell the Trial Chamber about that, and specifically, the conditions under which a family member or potential family member may be allowed to view a body in order to attempt to make an identification.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated, everything we described - the clothing, the height, and then the bullet found in the right leg, and especially a belt with a buckle that was very characteristic - the son identified the remains as those of his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zujo. I think now we're ready to move on to the next of your autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are the attachments to Dr. Zujo's 94 bis statement, which are marked F, G, and H. F being the English version, G being the French version, and H being the original language B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, I would like to direct your attention to your report of the exhumation and autopsy in respect of a body that was subsequently identified as that of Aziz Colakovic. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as was the case with the previous report that related to Nenad Harmandic, is this a report that was made by you and Dr. Dobraca and submitted to the high court in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report that you have in front of you was signed by Dr. Dobraca and myself because we jointly conducted the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then was this report subsequently made part of the proceedings in the courts in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was sent to the cantonal of the court in Mostar, to the investigative magistrate who had requested the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, the exhumation which resulted in your examination of this body, can you tell us the date of that exhumation and where the exhumation occurred?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exhumation took place on the 7 May, 1998, and it was conducted at the Sarica Harem I, which is a local cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us whether this body was exhumed from a single grave or from a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a single grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were other bodies exhumed from other single graves at the same location at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, we conducted multiple exhumations, first at the Sarica Harem, and then in other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I see from your report that this particular body was exhumed from a grave marked as NN number 96. Is that the number that was associated with this body during the course of the exhumation and autopsy? Or should I say, perhaps, that it was working number 01?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every grave is designated with a number, and as I explained yesterday, from the time of access, when we reach the spot, we put a number. And that corpse was number 96. And until it is buried, that number is used, and the body, when it is buried, of course, bears that number as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in the report which you made and submitted initially to the high court in Mostar, the cantonal court, there is an indication that this body had previously been delivered in March of 1994 by the HVO in Mostar, along with an additional number of bodies, approximately 72 in total. Are you in a position to tell us anything about the transfer of bodies from the HVO in March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that we received and recorded in the official minutes and report we obtained from the investigating Judge. And what was important for us was to see that an abduction had not been conducted on those bodies previously, which would make this a repeated autopsy. And that is why we say that on the 29th of March, there was an exchange - 1994 - that these corpses were exchanged. That's why it says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the record -- the English record indicates that you were concerned or you wanted to see that an abduction had not been conducted on these bodies previously. And I just want to clarify if that's the correct word, "abduction," is that the word you are intending to use?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Autopsy," interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the autopsy took place before, immediately after the exchange, whether an autopsy was performed on those corpses then, and after our own exhumation, it would be a repeated autopsy, re-autopsy, which means that we would look for the records and minutes and reports that were made earlier so that we could use them when we repeated the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you can say, and I don't know if you can, is it correct for us to assume, then, that this body had been buried at this location at the Sarica Harem cemetery since approximately March of 1994, when it had been delivered by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specify the time. All I can say is that the body was interred in a PVC bag, and that the body was completely skeletonised. And this tells us that the body had been exposed under an optimum temperature and optimum humidity so that the fatty tissues had turned into what we call soapy substance, and that is why we use this term "saponified." They are conservative changes, as we call them, where saponification takes place. Where there is a lot of air, we call it mummification, so they are the changes that a corpse undergoes due to the surrounding conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, I just want to make sure that we are clear on that because initially the English word we were given for the condition of the body was that it was "completely skeletonised," and then subsequently we were given the word "saponification." Now earlier, you described the body of Nenad Harmandic as having been "skeletonised" and I just want to make sure that we have got it correct in the transcript. The body that was subsequently identified as that of Aziz Colakovic, was it skeletonised or was there, as you have indicated, I believe, saponification?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number was 96, I believe. The ordinal number was 96. Colakovic Aziz, born in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The body of Aziz Colakovic, in your report, you say that you found a condition of post-mortem changes expressed in complete saponification of the body.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is different than skeletonisation?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. With a skeletonised corpse, the skin, the muscles, and all the internal organs have disappeared, disintegrated, which means that all that remains of the body is the skeleton, or rather, the bones. Whereas saponification, the skin muscles and internal organs change to a white mass and a soapy substance, it looks like soap, and that's why we call it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sopification or saponification, the interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that is the difference between the skeletonised state of a body and the saponification state of a body.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: With the white soapy substance, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, let me ask you first: Were you able to determine whether, in fact, there had been a prior autopsy on this body?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In going over your report, can you tell us, please, your finding -- tell us, please, first, the condition of the body in terms of the clothing and other general information which may have assisted subsequently in the identification of this body.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as clothing is concerned, on the dead body we found the sweat suit top and the combination of the colour was grey, blue-green, grey. There was also a cream-coloured V-necked T-shirt, a leather belt with a round buckle, blue jeans with a metal label, and the manufacturer was Unicon I, that was the brand. It had white wool socks and green Speedo swimming trunks. As to the footwear, there was just the remains of the toe of a shoe. No other items were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you able to determine approximately the age of this person at the time of death?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 25 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, could you tell us, please, what injuries, if any, you found and if you were able to determine the cause of death of this person. What was the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The injuries that we found when we performed the autopsy on the body, we found a fracture of the 8th rib on the right side of the thoracic cage, and a fracture of the right ulna in the lower third of its length. As for the mechanisms or what caused the injuries, we stated that parts of shells or shrapnels or bullets were the cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you recover any bullet or shrapnel from this body during the course of the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not find either a bullet or shrapnel during the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Does that suggest, then, that the bullet or shrapnel would have passed completely through the body?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, an entrance/exit wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How is it that you can determine that these fractures would have been caused by something like a bullet or piece of shrapnel as opposed to other fractures, say, those on the body of Nenad Harmandic which you characterised as having been caused by a blunt mechanical object? What are the different features in these fractures that would enable you to make this particular kind of finding?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are types of fractures. So the difference between the first body and the second body is that we found that the bone had been blasted, a limited blast to the bone, both in the region of the ulna and in the rib cage region. And that corresponded to parts of a shell or a projectile or bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in your opinion, can you shed any light on the relative position of the body, particularly the position of the ulna in respect of the rib cage at the time of impact? As we were dealing with a fracture of the right rib cage and right ulna, which means all on the same side, the right-hand side, within the area of the hand, tells us that part of the projectile or a shrapnel was done by one impact or one entrance/exit wound because the hand is mobile, you can place your hand in this kind of position. And it would have taken in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So are you saying, then, that the hand apparently had been placed close to the chest so that the single impact caused the same fracture to both the ulna and the rib, or do I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hand needn't be right up to the body, but it would be at a height of the 8th rib, whether it was closer to the body or further away from the body, we cannot say. But the ulna of the right hand was at the level of the 8th rib on the right-hand side. And this is the position. I can demonstrate by doing this movement [Indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then I take it from your report that the fractures themselves would not have been the specific cause of death; rather, the specific of death would have been the internal bleeding and external bleeding caused by the bullet or the shrapnel which had caused those fractures?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We state in our conclusion that the cause of death was violent, violent death through internal and external bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, how, then, it was determined that this body was, in fact, the body of Aziz Colakovic?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was the same as with the previous body. What we did was to contact the family members, and we learned from them what the person was wearing before he died, how old he was, how tall he was. And it was on the basis of all those indices and all our own findings - the external description of the corpse and the clothing and what we learned from his brother Salko - we identified him as being Aziz Colakovic, who was born in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So in other words, as was the case with Nenad Harmandic, a member of the family came and viewed the body and was able to make an identification, based on the various factors which you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But before he came -- he was brought into the room, the procedure was the same. We took down all this information, all the facts, and when we had ascertained the height, the state of the teeth, and all the other parameters used for reaching an identification, only then did we ask Salko into the room to identify the body of the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you made an initial, I guess tentative, finding, based on the information provided by the family and the information which you obtained during the course of the examination, that there was a sufficient link to justify bringing in a potential family member?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just have one moment, please. I believe I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have finished my line of questioning as to these two reports, and perhaps -- I'm not going to move ahead until the Trial Chamber has resolved the additional report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we proceed with the cross-examination on those two reports, and later on, if you decided that you will furnish us with more information as to the third report, then we will come back to your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Mr. Par, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start my cross-examination, I would like to have a document handed round which I will probably be using, so may I ask the usher's assistance to provide the parties with a copy, the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. And I shall provide the witness with the English version. This should be D2/24, the number, according to my calculations and records.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit Number D2/25.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, you will have time to read through this and the Croatian version. There won't be any problems, I'll give you enough time and explain what it is about. But let me start off by introducing myself. My name is Jelimir Par, attorney and Defence counsel for the accused Vinko Martinovic. We are going to discuss your testimony here today. To begin with, I omitted to see whether you had stated that you were a specialist in pathology, and forensic pathology in particular, within the framework of your field of expertise. Does that include those two areas?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a pure specialist in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: With respect to the exhumation of the corpse which you identified as Nenad Harmandic, I am going to ask you several questions, so we're going to focus on that particular exhumation. Could you begin by telling me what this looked like in practice? What was the team that conducted the exhumation? What were the team members, who was the team leader, and that kind of thing, when you conducted the exhumation? Could you enlighten me as to that, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Institute for Forensic Medicine received an order from the investigating Judge of the cantonal district of the court in Mostar, and the number was 399/ -- no 39/98, I apologise. 39/98 was the number, and the composition of the team was Dr. Dobraca, Dr. Zujo, and the assistants. We went to Mostar -- because we live in Sarajevo. We travelled to Mostar, and we had to wait for the investigating Judge, Munevera Rahimic, and Sabina Beganovic -- no, let me put myself right. Maksumic Halil was the Judge's name. And the crime technicians of the cantonal MUP and international representatives as well, they were on site; and the commission for the recovery of displaced persons as well, missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, who led your team? Was it you yourself or Dobraca or was there no team leader?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no team leader. It was a joint team, which means that the team went to Liska Park, the whole group, and they were personally present when the bodies were dug up and exhumed, the transportation of the bodies to Sutina and joint -- a joint effort during the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, who performs the actual autopsy; you, Dobraca, the two of you together? Could you tell us what this looks like in practice; what is the procedure?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I personally, I myself, conducted the autopsy. He took notes. He stood by the table, the autopsy table, and took down notes. So it was me, together with an assistant. I had the necessary clothes on and conducted the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The Harmandic case, that is the one I'd like to focus on now. As far as I understood, it wasn't a autopsy in the classical sense of the word because there was in fact no body, it was just the skeleton. So you examined the skeleton. Am I right in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is an autopsy. Exhumation means to exhume the body, that is, to take out the body. Inhume means to inter the body. And an autopsy is an autopsy because we had a corpse. We had the object of our forensic investigations, whether it is the entire body or just the skeleton, but the term "autopsy" applies to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have to control your pace of asking questions. Since you and the witness are speaking the same language, you really give a difficult time to the interpreters, and we all rely on the interpretation of what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'm not troubled by the terminological problem of "autopsy," but in practical terms, is it an examination of the bones or do you examine other things as well?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the autopsy is concerned, we have an external and internal examination. The external examination involves the description of the clothing and an examination of all the items found. All that is a component part of the autopsy process itself. Then we go on to the internal examination, where we conduct various measurements and examine the bones if you're only dealing with a skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So, you do nothing with the use of a scalpel, if I can put it that way? In the Harmandic case, we see nothing but the bones and the external examination. Do I understand you correctly? And please pause between my question and your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you exhume a body, you will always find the remnants of putrefication on the bone. And the muscles and all that have disintegrated, but it cloys to the bones themselves. But it is putrefied particles, and you have to use a scalpel to clean the bone from these additional material.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So everything begins with the exhumation, and you, as a team, attended the exhumation. My next question is the following: When you take the bones out, do you make a note of the position of the bones, do you measure their length, or do you just place them, as in this case, in a blanket or a piece of cloth or whatever? Could you explain that process to me. What do you do when you actually dig up a grave? How do you record what you find; the position of the bones, the measurements and so on? Could you explain that to me, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were personally present when the digging up took place. That is to say, when the soil, when the earth was dug up and we reached the corpse. The corpse, in this particular case, was surrounded by a blanket, so we photographed the blanket because we hadn't got to the corpse yet. And we used the same markings that were up above ground. So we photograph what we find when the earth is dug up, while the body is still in the grave, so you can see the position of the corpse, how the corpse was buried. If we are dealing with a skeleton and the bones, the position they are in; the position of the hands, whether they are tied or not and details of that kind, whether the corpse is clothed. But nothing is touched. You photograph the position with the blanket, and then you place the corpse, with the blanket, in the special bag used for corpses, and we write down the number and the number of the body. This body is then sent up to the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you take no measurements at that time; only photographs are taken.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in the grave itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And the investigative magistrate was also present during the exhumation, and what was her job there? And please, mind the pauses.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigative magistrate, she - in this case - takes note of those who attend the exhumation, then the location where the exhumation is to take place is described, and when the body is exhumed, a description is made of how it was found, what it was wrapped in, in this case. And then the technicians measure the depth and width of the actual grave, and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were -- was the family present at the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer that question because there were a number of members of various families around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Is it a common practice to have such presence?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We allow this. During the autopsy in certain cases, when we already know who is in question, and if they want to view this, if they want to attend it, we allow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, who interviewed the family members -- the members of the Harmandic family about the effects that could have been found there?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the crime technicians from the MUP who conducted it. And one of us always contacts these families.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you explain a little bit more about this, these interviews? There are various families, various members who are interested in this. So the crime technicians get certain information, but let's say you have a set of bones in this case. How do you know how to relate -- correlate it to a certain family who provided certain information? Can you again describe it in greater detail, if you can, how you do that in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forensic medicine, that is, we come there as experts, which means that the commission for the missing persons had received certain information and forwarded this information to the public Prosecutor in the cantonal court in Mostar, and then the Prosecutor pass it on to the Judge, to the magistrate, and so it went. Now, whether we alone would be involved in this, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What am I in fact really specifically interested in, it's this: When you conduct an autopsy, do you try to establish that this was really Nenad Harmandic, or you establish certain information, and then correlate this information with some other information that you have so that you see that it is actually the person in question? In this specific case, in the process of identification of these skeletal remains, did you already -- were you already in possession of this information? In other words, were you trying to confirm that these remains were really the remains of Nenad Harmandic, based on the information which you had previously received?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task is to assist the families in identification, that is, to assist them, and I said just a moment ago how we do that. That is, through the description of the personal items, the height, and certain specific information. In other words, we only assist in identification; we are not going to suggest -- we will not try to say no, this is the person. In other words, we provide assistance in identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. I think I understood it, the gist of it. But my question in fact was, as the person who performs autopsies, after you've performed one, you said -- you say afterwards, this is a person who may be about 45 years of age, maybe about 182, 83 centimetres tall, has a bullet, and then, based on that information, you say, do we have something that matches our findings? Can you answer me that, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before any regular autopsy of a fresh body - because we do autopsies daily - we have to take into account the circumstances that surround this case. What does that mean? We have to see the time, the manner of ensuring, the circumstances under which the person died. And in this case, when you talk about identification, for me, a very important detail, as I said yesterday, and I pointed out that I've conducted a lot of autopsies, it is -- we've done a lot of identification based on scar tissue. Let's say he had a fracture of the upper elbow bone, and through identifying the scar tissue, we can assist families in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So in the course of these autopsies that were conducted in Sarajevo, there were bodies that were not identified. Did you take DNA samples of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The practice is either at the institute, and during the examinations, when the -- an identification was made by the family, we don't take DNA samples. However, where we have John or Jane Does, we always take DNA samples. We take samples from the thigh bone, from a tooth, and we have various standards. Some ask that a piece of -- that the DNA be taken either from the thigh bone, in some other standards it is from the teeth, so we take both.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Regarding the injuries which you said were found on the body identified as Harmandic's, you said that these injuries were sustained during his life, such as the right thigh injury. Now, how can you establish, on the basis of a bone, that it was sustained during life, while the person was alive or after the person had died?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as fractures of bones are concerned, it is something as we -- you can see it by simply eye-balling it, as we say it in our trade. There are certain vital responses so that you can immediately say this was sustained while the person was alive and this was sustained after a person had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So in forensic medicines, this is not something that is in dispute?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, regarding the age, establishing the age, today you mentioned that this is done on the basis of seams or something between bones. What kind of a method is this?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the seams are concerned, the seams of the skull, it is clear when the ossification occurs, at what age. At the age of 70, these seams completely disappear. We also use pubic bones, or pelvic bones, and we look at the bumps. Also the collarbone or the thoracic cage bones, that is, ribs, are also examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, what is -- is this an exact method? To what degree of exactitude can this be determined?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The margin of error is five years, plus/minus, except with small children. But for adults, the margin of error is plus/minus five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I heard of a method through carbon analysis. Do you use that?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't use that. It is not something that we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Exact -- with other injuries which you enumerated there, you said that you identified some entrance/exit wounds of the face. Were you able to identify the entrance wound and the exit wound so that you would be able to determine the direction that the bullet came from? This is in general; you need not go to the specific case.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find the page. In this case, we established that it was the left cheekbone. It is this bone here [Indicating], which is separated out, and it is connected with the nose bone, and then with the temporal lobe. It is a bone that is between the two sets of bones. What we found was we found a round hole which would correspond to the entrance wound made by the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In these findings, you also mention that a bullet 6.35 millimetre calibre was found. Can you recall, where exactly was that discovered?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that it was found in the area of right thigh. I cannot tell you exactly whether this was the lower third, the upper third or where, because it was difficult to establish that because this putrid material was there, and we were unable to establish -- to pinpoint the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Was this found in the bone or in the tissue?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was found in the material that would correspond to the soft tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Was it attached to the bone?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was next to the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But you could not determine exactly where it was; upper third, lower, or where?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, we did not determine it because we had this putrefied material. We did not establish whether it was from the front, from the back; it was all in this material that was enveloping the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know where this bullet is now, where it is kept?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything we find, including projectiles and all the items, are taken into custody by the crime technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So on the basis of all this, exhumations and whatever was done, this should all be somewhere in Mostar, including the bullet and everything else?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the clothing is concerned, the clothing is taken and reburied with the body. But if we have something that is very specific, such as bullets, shrapnel, or some kind of nooses or things like that, that is kept. But the clothing is buried with the body, and often times, the family will take certain objects, such as a watch or a wallet, and they take it with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We mentioned here a leather belt with a buckle, a bullet, some remains of jeans. Would belt and buckle also be at the MUP with the crime lab or not?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the belt is concerned, often times the family will request certain items of clothing as mementos. I cannot tell you whether in this case the family asked for the belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My colleague reminded me, and I'll take you back to this bullet in the finding of Dr. Dobraca on page 4, it says that the bullet itself was found with the remains, but I cannot say in which position next to the body. This is now a little bit at odds with what you said.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the right thigh. This is our autopsy report, but I think I gave you the answer because when you asked a moment ago in which area of thigh, I told you that we could not establish that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you have this blue folder here? It's under E, for you, Tab E, page 4, that is in B/C/S. And it says, the bullet found -- this is Dr. Dobraca's finding. It says that it was found next to the body, but where it was --

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is consistent with what I have said, whether it was on the side. You see, if it's here, on the outside, I cannot say exactly because it was found in this putrefied material.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What I'm particularly interested in is it says here it was found near the body. This is what I wanted to point out, that in Dobraca's finding, that the bullet found with the remains was in the location near the body, which was not specific.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also said that I cannot say exactly where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, when you write these reports, who writes it? Does Dr. Dobraca write it or you write them?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is our joint report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I understand that the report is joint, but in actuality, who sat down and wrote it up?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating magistrate will call us to the court, and we will dictate the finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We also have a statement by Dr. Dobraca given to this Tribunal which contains a finding on an exhumation with his conclusions and everything. Is that also your joint statement or just his?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's joint.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell me, where is Dr. Dobraca now?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see, in Sarajevo. Does he continue to work as an expert and conduct these -- draft these reports?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Is he sick now or does he have any health problems?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of. He comes to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Is there a reason why Dr. Dobraca, who was slated to come here originally before this Tribunal, is there a reason why he couldn't come, why this substitution took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the question on the grounds of relevancy. The witness has been qualified as an expert. He has testified as the expert witness as to these issues. It's irrelevant as to why his colleague who authored these reports with him is not here in his place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par. You may skip the question. We believe that is irrelevant to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't get the interpretation, so I was unable to fully understand what my learned friend had said, but I understood what your ruling was so I'm going to move on. However, I believe that it is relevant for our Defence why Dr. Dobraca did not appear here. In fact, I can tell the Trial Chamber and see whether I will be allowed to pursue this. Dr. Dobraca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would object to this practice as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, what you are going to say has nothing to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness and Dr. Dobraca work as a team and jointly sign findings, including the findings that we have here. And they both stand by their findings. I have certain information which I was going to put to Dr. Zujo which may point out to possible reasons why Dr. Dobraca is not here. We received information from the Prosecution that Dr. Dobraca could not attend due to some illness. I am trying to verify this with this witness without trying to put this witness in any kind of awkward position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, this witness may know or may not know about the reason why the other doctor has not appeared before this Tribunal. But it has nothing to do with the testifying of this witness at all. You will have the full right to call that doctor. If he failed to come, you may explain the reason for that in your case of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President. However, I believe that this witness is defending a finding of Dr. Dobraca. I want to ask a question on the credibility of Dr. Dobraca as expert because we believe that that is one of the reasons why he did not appear here. And I wanted to ask this witness because this is their joint finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time, you know, at this moment. Shall we break, and later on we come back to this subject. Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness out first. We'll resume at 11.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, would you inform the Chamber about your reason of asking that question, in the absence of the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. The object of my questioning, and to test the credibility of Dr. Dobraca, is based on, if I can put it that way, an affair, an incident, which was public knowledge linked to Dr. Dobraca's expertise during the war. In the press, in a well-known daily, Slobodna Bosna, the 24th of September, 1998, that is a Sarajevo daily, and also in another daily, called Slobodna Dalmacija, of the 12th of September, 2000, an interview appeared by a certain Edin Garaplija. Edin Garaplija was a former member of AID who worked in Sarajevo. During the war -- rather, after the war, this man Edin Garaplija was detained, and he was sentenced to a prison term in Sarajevo. After he was sentenced to a term of imprisonment, he began talking about what had happened in Sarajevo during the war, how AID worked and similar things. And among other things, he said that there were certain liquidations of persons which were executed - I don't want to say by whom - but that these liquidations were covered up by the fact that false autopsies were performed. And he also claims that certain persons were liquidated by injections that were administered. He states the name of a man who conjured up these poisons for the needs of AID, and he claims that Dr. Dobraca at that time was an -- conducted autopsies, and these liquidations or these deaths were falsified in his reports and made to look as if they were deaths by natural causes. So this all came out as a series of interviews by this man called Edin Garaplija and they appeared in the press. Furthermore, according to information and facts that I have at my disposal, this man, Edin Garaplija in order to clarify his case, contacted a specific court body which exists in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is called the human rights centre for Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in a case which, as far as I know was called Garaplija versus the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have the number of that trial - it is CH 98/934 - this man Garaplija stipulates -- sets out these facts about the false autopsies that were conducted. I personally, therefore, was not able to have insight into these court documents. I received the judgement in the -- of the case, but as it was not contended, I personally have no personal knowledge of what the court documents contain. But as far as the newspaper articles are concerned, I can say at this point that, although I don't have the newspapers themselves, I have excerpts from the internet with the facts as to what was stated, and I remember following and reading about this affair when it was -- when it appeared in the press. Therefore, what I wanted to achieve today with my questioning of this witness, of Dr. Zujo, was the following: I think - and I'm not going to enter into the correctness of the allegations made by the man Garaplija, I don't know whether that is true or not, but it was an affair that was public knowledge, and it could have burdened -- placed a burden on Dr. Dobraca and was perhaps a reason why he did not appear in court here. I wanted to ascertain that, whether that was indeed the reason. And I don't think that we can have a replacement for him and have Dr. Zujo alone to cover this subject matter whereas the head of the team, the institute, and Dobraca, quite obviously, does not wish to appear. So the question of the credibility of Dr. Dobraca is what I wanted to test on the basis of the information I have at my disposal. That is by way of explanation, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what we are concerned in this trial is the relevance of what you said to this very case. That means, to this autopsy report. Are you challenging the credibility and authenticity of this autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this, Your Honour: It is not easy for me to say whether I question it, challenge it, or not. But the general premise of our Defence case is the following, And it relates to this matter: That different services, first and foremost, AID, were at work here in order to prepare evidence, if I can put it that way. So through that prism, we -- and spectrum, we are testing the ways and means of the preparation of all this, and witnesses as well. In this particular case, we challenge that the body is indeed the body of Mr. Harmandic. We are trying to prove and show that the autopsy that was conducted and the identification was not a proper one and that it was not Harmandic's body. And through this process of discreditation of the physician conducting the autopsy - and we have certain knowledge about this physician; that he was working in the service or on orders from the AID - and that therefore, according to that information, those autopsies, if I can say so, were false. That is something that we would like to link up and -- in order to challenge the report, to challenge the correctness of the report and to challenge the fact that the corpse was indeed the corpse of Mr. Harmandic. That is our position. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let us hear the response from the other side. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, my first remark, I think, comes from the very first sentence that counsel stated at the beginning of his comments, which was they want to challenge the credibility of Dr. Dobraca. Dr. Dobraca is not the witness in this case. Dr. Zujo is the witness. And I think it's not helpful to attempt to challenge the credibility of someone who is not a witness before the Trial Chamber. That's number one. We have one witness, Dr. Zujo. We have two autopsies; the autopsy of what is submitted to be the body of Harmandic, and what is submitted to be the body of Aziz Colakovic. Now, the witness, Dr. Zujo, as he has testified, is a joint author of each of the autopsy reports which are a part of the 94 bis statement. His signature appears on each of those, as well as the signature of Dr. Dobraca, but he is a joint author, and I think it's clear that before the Trial Chamber he has affirmed and adopted those reports as his own. Those are the reports themselves. Among the other attachments to the 94 bis statement is the OTP witness statement of Dr. Dobraca marked as Exhibit D, the English version; Exhibit E, the version in B/C/S. Now -- and we can ask the witness about this on the face of the document, the witness statement. The Court will find that Dr. Zujo was present during this interview. And I believe that, if asked, the witness would also say that his signature or his initials appear on the witness statement. So I think that the witness has also signed and adopted this witness statement jointly with Dr. Dobraca. We could pursue that with the witness if it's deemed to be necessary. Finally, we have the 94 bis statement itself, signed in October of last year by the witness, Dr. Zujo. He is the witness. And it's for those reasons that we believe it's not useful or it doesn't shed any light on his testimony to attempt to impeach someone who is not the witness. Secondly, as I mentioned, there are two autopsies. If it's the Defence assertion that either of these two autopsies was, as counsel -- to use counsel's phrase, a false autopsy, we would have no objection to the Defence putting that to the witness, challenging these autopsies on the grounds or the assertion that this autopsy or the Colakovic autopsy was in fact a false autopsy or that these people in fact died or were liquidated by the Bosnian secret service. If they want to confine their inquires along those lines to the two autopsies that were tendered to the Trial Chamber, there won't be objections from the Prosecution as to that line. But the line that they apparently want to go down is to impeach someone who is not a witness with allegations regarding autopsies which are not in this case. And so it's -- and let me add, in my final comment, and I listened carefully to counsel's remarks, we have yet to hear any assertion that Dr. Zujo's credibility is being challenged by the Defence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mladen Naletilic, as we are dealing with points 1 and 2 up until 5, counts 1 to 5, has to do with Mladen Naletilic. I didn't want to put forth my own opinions but I see that I have to now. I didn't respond to my learned colleague yesterday although the comment I made was quite clear. Your Honours, we are dealing with a classic lack of understanding of the system. My colleague Mr. Par and the rest of the Defence counsel from the territories of the former Yugoslavia lived in a system in which, when we are talking about forensic medicine, there is the head of pathology, the head of forensic medicine, and then we have their subordinate, subordinate physicians. No autopsy report, regardless of whether they were done by the subordinates, could have left the institute without the signature of the head of the service; and if the head of the service conducted the autopsy - Your Honours, this is the truth - it is the practice that we all know; Mr. Seric was a Judge for 20 years, we have all been attorneys for over 20 years, and we listen to these distinguished expert witnesses every day in our courtrooms. We know our court practice. And what Mr. Par just said was perhaps not well explained because of the difference of the systems. If Mr. Dobraca was the head of the team, then the autopsy report is his and not Dr. Zujo's. Dr. Zujo could only have signed the autopsy report as a second signature, but it is not his autopsy report; it is the autopsy report of Dr. Dobraca. I don't know if I have been able to explain the system as it stood and as it functioned and the way in which our experts work. But if you find that necessary, then the Defence counsel will bring in those same forensic experts to explain the situation and the differences in system. So if the witness isn't here, I cannot disqualify him. Perhaps that is possible; perhaps not. This is my first encounter with the system. We are not challenging the credibility of Dr. Zujo at all, and that is why Dr. Dobraca was not brought by the Prosecution because he would have been discredited because there is too much public information and data from the human rights court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I even think the investigations of this particular Tribunal and this particular Prosecution and OTP because it was an organisation which was called Sheva [phoen] which is the subject of this investigation, the investigations of this Tribunal, and Dr. Dobraca was the one who masked the real cusses of death. So I don't know, Your Honours, if I have been able to explain the situation to you sufficiently, but I wanted to assist my colleague in his explanations, why Mr. Par, my learned colleague, and myself, consider that we were perfectly right and in order to present our views as we have done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, you have to be very concise, because this kind of debate is going on for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Simply to respond to one assertion made by my learned friend Mr. Krsnik; the Prosecution did not fail to bring Dr. Dobraca for the reasons which have just been asserted. Footnote one of the 94 bis statement states that the Prosecutor had originally intended to call Dr. Dobraca, which was the case, but that the Prosecutor is informed that, due to health problems Dr. Dobraca is not able to testify. That's all we know, Mr. President. The rest of all these assertions, I don't know anything about them, but the reason, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, as to why Dr. Dobraca is not here is as we have stated in the 94 bis statement, due to health problems that we were informed of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one sentence, with your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, this Trial Chamber believes that you have the full right to challenge the credibility and authenticity of those autopsy reports. You could ask any questions to this witness to that direction. But we also notice that Dr. Dobraca is not a witness of this case. We also notice that those reports are signed by two doctors, and Dr. Zujo is one of the authors of those reports. He should be responsible for whatever is said in those reports. So we kindly ask you to skip the questions concerning with Dr. Dobraca in this respect. And at a later stage, maybe in the case of the Defence in the future, you have the full right to bring over your expert witness to attack the evidence presented today by the Prosecution. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have understood your instructions, and I will proceed accordingly. I have just one question: If I should decide -- or rather, if we should decide, as the Defence team, in the course of the Defence case to call Dr. Dobraca and he refuses to come, can we ask the Trial Chamber's assistance and the Trial Chamber could call the witness as a court witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure whether the witness will be called as a court witness or not, but I can assure you that the Chamber will do its best to help you, even issuing some orders in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before the witness comes back in, I can inform the Trial Chamber of our position as to Mustafa Krilic. We reviewed the record during the break. We found reference to Professor Krilic in two witnesses. However, we think that in light of a number of factors, including the shortness of time remaining in our case, the fact that the evidence regarding Krilic is not central to the allegations in the case, we are ready, Mr. President, to proceed without taking testimony regarding the autopsy report of Professor Krilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, before we bring in the witness, we may not have made it perfectly clear to you what you should do -- just take the witness out for a moment. And you may not have understood: When this witness comes back, obviously you will conduct your cross-examination in whatever way you elect, but you should put specifically to this witness the contents and the findings of the experts' report that you handed up to him. And obviously, you can ask him specific questions, because it wouldn't be fair not to put those questions to him and only put them later on in the Defence case. So I mean, some of the findings are obviously something that needs to be teased out and parsed by expert witnesses, so just in case you misunderstood, you must put the findings of your expert to this particular expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the intention of my cross-examination, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Zujo, the Court has made a ruling in the meantime, and I will not be asking you questions regarding Dr. Dobraca that I asked you a moment ago. We're going to focus on something else, but before we go on to another area, I should like to ascertain whether you are the cosignatory of all these findings that Dr. Dobraca made, all the ones that we have before us and that were sent to us by the Prosecution. Were you the cosignator with Dr. Dobraca, including the statement made by him to the Office of the Prosecutor? Do you sign them as being your own as well? Are you the cosignatory?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all our joint findings, and I signed all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Including the statement given to the Tribunal? This is what I have in mind, what I'm talking about. It is the statement of Ilijas Dobraca to the Tribunal, which contains facts about exhumations, the conclusion, the opinions, findings.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have my signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you assert that, do you?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That completes that area of questioning. Let's move on. I don't know if you have received a copy in Croatian -- or rather, the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to provide Mr. Zujo a copy of the document, and I shall, of course, give him time to look through it and tell him what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Before you begin, let me just tell you what the document is. The Defence of Vinko Martinovic, with the aim of preparing this cross-examination, provided your findings and Dr. Dobraca's findings to Dr. Professor Josip Skavic. Do you know who Dr. Josip Skavic is?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is professor of the faculty of medicine in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, and a leading expert in forensic medicine and the area you delve in, so you know that he is an authority in the that particular field. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We have asked Dr. Skavic to give his opinion, to state his opinion. The document contains several pages. Would you read through it, and then I would like to ask you some questions about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters have asked for the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I have provided them with a copy, but if not, I have additional copies. I have copies in English, and this is in Bosnian. Would the usher please assist me in providing them with a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to the section entitled "Opinion." That was on page 3 of the Bosnian/Croatian version. The first element or factor that Dr. Skavic considered was the height of this body which is purported to be the one of Harmandic. It was not clear how the expert calculated the assumed height of the body. Today, you gave us your explanation, but he gave his own calculation, taking into account your measurements, and he came with the height of 185.08 centimetres. You arrived at a slightly different measurement. How do you explain this discrepancy, the difference between these two measurements?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, we took parameters. I read what Dr. Skavic said. We took the parameters, which included the diameter of the skull, which is taken from here to here [Indicating]. In some cases, the skull is sawed off, and then you take the measurement of the diameter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person is built proportionately, then the proportion of the diameter in millimetres will correspond to the height of the body in centimetres. Here we found the diameters to be 180 millimetres, which would correspond to 180 centimetres of body height. That was one parameters. The other parameter was the femur or the thighbone, and we found that that shaft was 50 centimetres long. Then we take this number, which is then multiplied by a factor 3.66, and you get a value which would be approximately 183 to 185. We also measured the humerus or the upper arm bone, and we found it to be 36 centimetres long. That is then multiplied by the factor of 5.06, and you get a value of the length. All these measurements have a margin of error of several centimetres, so we took a median value and we said that the length of the body was 182 to 85 centimetres, which allowed us a possibility to add the margin of 2 to 5 centimetres, which is standard in the literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Are these plus/minus margins or do you add on that value?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you add it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So it's only a plus value?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you deal with skeletal remains, it's only a plus, an addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. In the case of Harmandic and in the case of Aziz Colakovic, if you can refer to your blue file folder, as I noted it in the Harmandic case, the thigh bone was 50?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 52. It is 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let me see what it says here. I think it was 50. It was 50, and Colakovic 52.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Colakovic was 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's go to Colakovic first. Colakovic is 52, and then the upper arm bone 37. And in Harmandic's case, 50, the thigh bone, and 36 the upper arm bone. However, their heights are different. In Colakovic's case, it is 187 to 190; and in Harmandic's case, the height established was 182 to 83. My question to you is I see these small differences, 2 to 3 centimetres in length of the bones, and the total height of the person, it would seem that Harmandic would appear to be taller even though his bones are a bit shorter. Did I misunderstand you or is there an inconsistency in your finding?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the error is in your interpretation. In Harmandic's case, the length -- that is, the diameter of the skull is 180. That is the diameter of the skull. The thigh bone is 50, and the upper arm, 36. And in Colakovic's case, the diameter of the skull is 170; the thigh bone 52, and the upper arm bone, 37. What I'm trying to say, when I spoke earlier that there are people who have large heads, proportionately to their bodies, and vice versa; small head, longer bodies. So when we calculate it, in Aziz Colakovic's case, the length of his body was over 185 centimetres. It is approaching 190. Because it states that the thigh bone, if it is 50, then it translates into 185 centimetres length of the full body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So his thigh bone, it was 52.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that corresponds to 190.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So your answer is that the same method was used, and your mathematics brings those consistent results?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, taking into account professor Skavic's findings, this finding of 185.08 centimetres, is that also an acceptable calculation to you? Do you agree with this or do you think that Skavic miscalculated and that your calculation is correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I could see, Professor Skavic used the same tables, and there's no deviation in his case. So that it would be the length, because here, he says the thigh bone of 50, and if we take the factor 3.66, which is typical for male, that's what we could see. Other authorities Zecevic, Pejakovic, and others, they all use the same tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In other words, you agree, more or less, about the height?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Considering the fact that Harmandic's son stated that his father was 190 centimetres tall, Dr. Skavic said that this calculation was absolutely uncertain. Do you agree with that conclusion, based on that factor alone?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have no other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, perhaps the word "factor" created confusion. When I said factors, I was thinking more like clothing and other items or things. But is it acceptable to you what Dr. Skavic concluded? He said that the identification, based on the height as calculated in this way, is absolutely not conclusive. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no other methods. If we have skeleton alone, this is the only method we have available. The diameter of the skull, the length of the thighbone, of the upper arm bone, those are the only things we can measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you, but I think that it was again my mistake in not being clear enough. Let me try to do it again. The difference between the 196 centimetres as given by Harmandic's son and your calculation of -- that is, 185.08 centimetres that Skavic found, that is a total of 11 centimetres difference. That is a difference too large to provide a clear standard for identification. In your opinion, is this the case, that on the basis of these factors, such identification cannot be made to appear conclusive?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could only use these parameters, which means the measurements and then the calculation, in order to come up with a certain height. When I said that the margin of error may be 5 centimetres, and because we are only dealing with a skeleton, we can add another 5 centimetres. I saw that some other experts who work for the Tribunal allow for a wider margin. For instance, I had an opportunity to see reports in which larger margins were used. But let me give you detail: A person who is 30 years of age starts losing his height each year, on average, 0.06 centimetres. So if somebody says that somebody was 186 centimetres tall, if this person is actually 185, that is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Well, they could have said 198. But does this tell us that it is not a certain way of measuring, that the difference is too big, the difference of 10 or 11 centimetres would point to two different persons?
