Can we agree that only if we take into account the height as a factor, that it is uncertain?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have no other method.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We all agreed that the method is acceptable, but I have still not received an answer. Let's take a practical example. We have an autopsy and a member of family says, This is -- the man was 186 centimetres tall, and you say, My measurements show 185. Can we say that a person who is -- 19 blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who, according to your measurements, is 186 can also be perhaps 196? Can we stretch it to 10 centimetres difference --

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have 5 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: -- which we can add?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I added it up front. With that addition, we still have a margin of 10 or 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I am not trying to torment you here with this, but I am asking you, if we only take the height as the method, as a factor, is it a method that can establish the identity with full certainty?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of height alone, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, forgive me for interrupting you but I think it's crucial that we need your assistance at this stage -- or I do anyway. Your challenge to the findings of this autopsy report are based on the report of the expert from Zagreb that you very kindly furnished us with. And his view appears to be based, as indeed is your cross-examination, on Mr. Harmandic's son stating that his father had a certain height. Where do we as Judges find this information? You see, we are continuing on this very interesting fact, but we don't have this information. Where did you get this information from? And where did your professor in Zagreb get the information from?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, are you referring to the information that Harmandic's son provided as the height of his father?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the information you're referring -- you see, we don't have that, and where would we find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Zujo can confirm that piece of information. If I understood Dr. Zujo, this is information furnished by the family at the time of exhumation because they expect to find their loved ones there, and the expert asked what was the height of this person. And in this particular case, the height indicated was 196. This was noted down by the expert, and then during the autopsy, this was taken into account on the basis of information provided by Harmandic's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm afraid we did not get translation from French.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We hear it on number 5, not 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Judge Clark can hear perfectly, anyway, on channel 5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're not on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We still didn't get the interpretation. There is some technical problem with the channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We can hear you on...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? The interpreter is asking if you can hear the English interpretation. Right, good, so we can do it now. Channel 4. Judge Diarra, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Par, I was telling you that Professor Josip was referring to some documents, and he based his opinions on those documents in order to make his analysis or his report. Those documents are not annexed to his report, which basically does not help us to understand this report very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is our omission. These are the same documents that are being used today. These were Prosecution documents, that is, the autopsy reports, and these are the same documents that are in front of you. These are the same documents that were used by Professor Skavic. He had no other documents in use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, but we don't have -- unless I'm being particularly obtuse, we don't have any documents that refer to information which Dr. Zujo received from the family in relation to this man's height. That's what we're intrigued by. Where do you -- you haven't even elicited in cross-examination or furnished a document which says that Dr. Zujo received this information that the son said that his father was 196 centimetres. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. I received that information from Dr. Zujo. So perhaps I should ask Dr. Zujo this, because he and Dr. Dobraca wrote that. This is information that they had received before the autopsy, because they were told that -- they were given this information from the family members. Perhaps we should give Dr. Zujo an opportunity to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, you heard the exchange. I think that you are the most competent person to give us an answer to this question. How do we have the initial height of Nenad Harmandic as being 196 high? How did we arrive at that?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in front of me the autopsy reports, and that height was not recorded in the report. However, when you canvass the family, when you say -- they say something like, "He was tall," but they will never tell us he was -- he had 196. They will say he was over 190 tall. But I have the autopsy report in front of me. I did not find that detail that it was 196.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, well, you calculated based on that information. I did not give that information to Dr. Skavic arbitrarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, the report from Professor Skavic suggests in its body that, when the professor was preparing his report, that he [redacted]. But there's no suggestions -- the point I'm making -- that this professor had -- [redacted] [redacted] in relation to the height when he was preparing the report. That's the problem I have. I was wondering if you could help me with that. Perhaps if we asked this witness what information was he given prior to autopsy, and did he record it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe that is not the right time, but I have to point out, concerning with the report from Dr. Skavic, that is the document you furnished to us, we have some doubts about this report because its lack of corroboration from other sources. First, if you are going to tender this document into evidence, we need the letters addressed to this doctor by Mr. Seric. Secondly, all those enclosed information in the documents; and thirdly, [redacted], [redacted], we need all those documents so that we could work along it. Maybe that's the subject we will come across with the issue of tendering of those documents into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President. We'll deal with that when the time comes. Let me go back to Judge Clark's question, and I think she clarified some points which I omitted to mention. I have here, I'm holding in my hand, and we can place it on the ELMO, perhaps, the statement by [redacted] which we received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [redacted] and he speaks about the height of the body. And on the last page, he says that the body of his father was 196 centimetres tall. We could place that on the ELMO, this portion, and then we can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go into private session for one quick moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are in the open session. You may proceed, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Zujo, let us move on, and according to Professor Skavic's opinions, we now come to the section in which he speaks about the factor of identification on the basis of clothing, clothing as a factor of identification. And he states -- and he, like you, as you know, during the war in Croatia, over a period of ten years, he conducted thousands of identifications in the same way. And he says that that is one of the methods used, the methods of identification, that is, clothing. But he says that his experience in his ten-year experience of the victims of the war for the homeland is that very often persons would exchange clothing so that, quite frequently, clothing identifying one person would be found on the body of another person, or several people, so that he considers that identification along those lines would not be sure enough, because experience tells him that clothing is not a very certain indicator of identification. What has been your experience in that area?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That first -- it is the first element of identification. Now, what does that mean? Usually, close family members tell us what the person was wearing. But the professor states very correctly that this cannot serve us at all times, nor do we have always something specific like the belt in this case. And the belt was specific for purposes of identification. But we have no other methods, so these are our initial methods, the first method. We describe the clothing, and then we consult the family members to see if those items of clothing correspond to the clothing mentioned by the family members. So that is what I have to say on the subject of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the belt as specified by the family members. In this courtroom, we heard testimony from a witness -- we don't want to disclose his identity, but he testified on the 26th of September, 2001. He was Witness U, and he spoke about the Harmandic case, and he said that in the Heliodrom where they were detained, that the belts were confiscated. We heard this from other witnesses later on, whether they were confiscated from everybody or from only certain persons, this particular witness did state that the belts were taken away from the detainees. And we asked this particular witness that and he allegedly saw Harmandic on the day he disappeared, and we asked him how Harmandic was dressed, and this is what he said: He said that Harmandic was wearing short white pants and a white T-shirt with short sleeves. So this testimony testifies to different clothing worn by Harmandic if we compare it to the clothing on the basis of which his body was identified. Now, had you had that piece of information at the time, would you still have -- would your identification have taken a different road? Would you have done some DNA analysis or something similar?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you understood me quite correctly when I said that the role of me in identifying a corpse was to assist the family. I never said that I would suggest to the family or to take a different road where I could do something negative. It is always my task to assist family members in the process of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I understand. So you don't say this is it; you don't claim that this is how things stand but you try and combine what you hear from them and what you tell them for them to be able to accept all this as part of what they already know. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question for you now is, do you take into account a specific psychological state which quite certainly appears in cases where persons are missing, where family members spend years looking for their nearest and dearest, and when they are not at rest, and then when we wish to find the body so that they could give their family member a proper funeral and put it behind them, and that they are prone, in one way or another, to accept what you tell them, especially in identification cases of this kind where we have no body but just the bones, that they are very willing to confirm something to end this personal drama of theirs. Have you come across cases of that kind and in the course of your practice, did you have cases in which there were repeated autopsies or something of that kind? Could you give us your views and experience on the subject. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the methods of identification earlier on, and I stated first and foremost that we undertake a description first. First of all, we describe what we find, all the external traits and internal traits during the autopsy. Everything is described and photographed, so these are assistant auxiliary methods, photography and so on. When I have completed all that, I tell the family, having asked them what the -- their family member was wearing, I say I have found such and such, does that coincide? Does it correspond to what you know? Height and so on. And only then do I take the family members into the autopsy room for them to be able to see for themselves the state of the body and that a corpse exists. So that is the final stage, the disclosure of the corpse. Now, why is that the final stage? It is precisely because of the psychological state that the family members are in, because they are family members who are not medically trained. They have had no contact previously, perhaps, with corpses, dead bodies. And as soon as they enter the autopsy room, they usually break out into tears. I have to prepare the family members before they enter the autopsy room to prepare them to view the body. So that is the final stage and final method of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Final, but decisive, is that right? If they say, yes, it is, and if it comes out with what you know, that is all right, that is the end of it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before they enter the autopsy room, unless all the details correspond to what they have said and what I have found, then I say to them, This does not correspond, our findings do not correspond to the body of your family member; and in that case, there's no need for them to go into the autopsy room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor, that is clear to me. But these are situations -- border situations; they can be, but needn't be. We are talking about a skeleton, that's all we have. What is decisive then? Is the final say of the family members decisive? That's how I understand it. So it is not on the basis of an analysis, which would take into consideration all the different factors. So there is always a certain measure of uncertainty, is that right, in which the family members have the definite say?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how the team conducting an exhumation is composed. You don't only have the forensic expert; you have the crime technicians and crime police, you have the investigating Judge, you have the Prosecutor. They are all present so that all the family members must talk to all the members of the team, because the investigating Judge has the final say in the exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor, I understand what you're telling me. I understand it all. But what I want to ascertain here is that the bones that you identified, employing the method that you employed, as being the body of Nenad Harmandic, I say that on the basis of what we are analyzing - the clothing factor, the height factor, the location of the bullet factor - all those factors cannot tell us with absolute certainty whether they are Harmandic's bones. It is only a DNA analysis which could tell us with top -- a top measure of certainty whether they are or not. All the rest is a combination of factors, combination of scientific facts, the family members and the need to find the body of that particular man. So my question to you is the following: In your opinion, is this a 100 percent proof identification, or can you not have 100 percent certainty unless you carry out a DNA analysis? That is all I am asking you. That is what I am trying to arrive at.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A DNA analysis is the foolproof method, the surest and most conclusive method, and we carry out DNA analyses. But when it is an unknown person, and yes, the DNA method is the best, most foolproof method.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, what do you have to say to the findings by Professor Skavic? Is that absolutely acceptable? Do you have any comments to make? Can you say that Skavic was wrong in this section of his analysis or, according to what he had at his disposal, would you say that the analysis was acceptable? What is your view on this report? Do you find it acceptable or not?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the findings made by the professor. I cannot state my views as to its acceptability or not. That is up to the Trial Chamber to judge. I have read it. I think that it does not deviate in any way from the findings because he mostly bases his analysis on lengths, and he cannot conjure up other formulas but the formulas that I have here. They are formulas which are well known in the world today. There are no other formulas for calculating the length of a corpse on the basis of lengths of the bones. So if he added 1 centimetre and so on, this margin is acceptable. I have said that the margin could even be 5 centimetres, as high as 5 centimetres, so you don't need any further opinions on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So it does not deviate from your scientific views from what you did. Can I take you to have said that?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that I do not wish to give my opinion any further than what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zujo. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Zujo. My name is Chris Meek, and I'm one of the counsel for Mr. Mladen Naletilic. I just have a few questions. A little bit confused on the exhumation process. You indicated, I believe, that at the actual cemetery where the body is exhumed, that there are many crime technicians, policemen, examining Judge, and a Prosecutor present besides you and the other doctor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And are the family members questioned and spoken to by the different individuals - such as the Prosecutor, the Judge, the police - prior to or after the body is actually exhumed?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before exhumation, they have the facts; that is to say, there is the commission for searching for missing persons. They have their files. And those files include all the details about the missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then the actual body that is exhumed is still in the ground when all these questions are asked to the family. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the body is exhumed, that is to say, the commission for searching for missing persons receives information, and then the commission sends them on to the Prosecution of the cantonal or district court, and the Prosecutor forwards them to the investigating Judge. The investigating Judge issues an order whereby the exhumation is to be conducted. And we, as the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Sarajevo, receive that order from the Judge, and the full team goes out to the exhumation site on a given date and day and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony this morning that your measurements are based on a proportionality of a person's body. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the bodies are fresh, we measure the length from head to toe. But if we're only dealing with a skeleton, then we use parameters of the kind that I have already described; the diameter of the head, the upper leg, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from the family of Mr. Harmandic that he was built proportionally?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You also indicated in your testimony that every person -- I believe, and I want you to correct me if I am wrong -- that every person, after they turn 30 years of age, begins to lose height at an average of .06 centimetres a year. Was that your statement?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is that for every one of us; you, me, and everybody in this courtroom and in this world?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you -- your specialty is forensic medicine, but you're also a medical doctor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of medicine first, and later on, my specialist training was forensic medicine as a pure specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that every human being has a certain amount of a growth hormone, and that some people lack that growth hormone?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is considered that the thymus gland, which is located here [Indicating], takes part in growth. And from age 16 upwards, it ceases. The thymus becomes fatty tissue and disappears after age 16. During an autopsy, if I find just a little -- I find just a portion of that fatty tissue. Now, if after age 16, it is retained, that means that we have a disturbance in growth and everything else because they are internal secretion glands. It is the endogenous system of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I take it with these skeletal remains, you didn't have that opportunity in this case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we only discovered the skeleton, which means that the muscles and all the bodily organs had decayed, and all that was left was around the bone but it was all decayed matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Doctor, that some people who have an excess of the growth hormone can continue to grow, even after they are 30 years old or even after they are 40 years old?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the hyperthymesis, and that is the director of all internal secretion glands, and the hyperthymesis -- if the full section of the hyperthymesis flourishes due to an excess of tissue and there are tumors, then we have acromegalia of the jaw and hands, the extremities. You have had occasion to see people with large, elongated jaws. That is what we call acromegalia, or this enlargement of the extremities, the fingers. But this is a result of disorder of the hyperthymesis. And usually adenoma, which are tumors in the hyperthymesis area and the foresection of the hyperthymesis, so in those cases, that can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony correctly, Doctor, you didn't have a lower jaw to examine in this case, did you?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was the lower jaw in our findings, and the teeth of the lower jaw. But not the upper teeth. We were not able to see the upper teeth in the upper jaw because the upper jaw was fractured. There were multiple fractures. But yes, we did have a lower jaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In regards to the exhumation and autopsy of Aziz Colakovic, I want you to go straight to your conclusion, if you will. It starts with: "The injuries to the rib and ulna were most likely the result..." Do you see that paragraph, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, from your autopsy on this body, that you could not -- could not establish within a reasonable medical certainty the cause of death but that you basically concluded that it was "most likely" or "most probably," but not within a reasonable medical certainty?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The injuries that we found with Aziz Colakovic were a fracture of the 8th rib and a fracture of the ulna, right ulna. And we said that these were injuries inflicted by a part of a shell, or a projectile from a firearm. We based this upon the fact that the injuries were limited, and they were characteristic of injuries inflicted with this type of weapon. As far as the rest is concerned, bleeding existed, and we said most probably that this bleeding was the direct cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Which are you talking about; are you talking about a bullet or are you talking about shrapnel or are you talking about a fragmentation? What is it exactly? Can you tell us within a reasonable medical certainty?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said in our findings that most probably they were fragmentations of bombs or shells or a bullet fired from a firearm, so we weren't able to say 100 percent as to the exact portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's 1.00. Thank you very much. I have maybe a question or two after lunch is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please bring the doctor out of the room first. We'll resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 13.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. How are you?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you, I'm well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I only have a few more questions. I would like you to clear up the bullet that you claim that you found in this bag, the body bag. That's where you found it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I hesitate to interject, but I think it would be useful to know whether, in light of the last remark from counsel, whether the Defence for Naletilic disputes the fact that the bullet was found with the body. I think there has been debate about the location and its significance, but the last remark was that -- indicated to me that counsel is disputing whether the bullet was found at all. And if that's the case, I think that he should put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe there's some follow-up questions put forward by Mr. Meek later on. You may proceed, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For my learned colleague, I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Doctor, you testified you that found a bullet with this body or near this body of Harmandic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the autopsy, we found a projectile, calibre 6.35, in the area of the right thigh, and I think that that is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, where is this projectile or bullet today?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that crime technicians of the police also worked there. Any bullet, shrapnel, and such, as a rule, they take, and they -- they take with them for expertise with the police. And so this is in the cantonal police in Mostar. Let me just add that the bullet was also photographed, and the photo album is an integral part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Doctor, you understand that we've only been provided with the report of your autopsy findings and the report of your colleague that you initialled -- no, I take that... Let me ask this question, Doctor: You indicated that the police officers and investigators would talk to the family first to determine what they could -- what information they could give the police and officials in regards to items of clothing, for example. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already pointed out the method of identification. That means that the starting point was the commission for missing persons, and then the police got involved, and then the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you know whether or not the police would have had or generated a report of any statements made by the family members regarding what types of things to look for to identify their loved one?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such information because that is a police matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would it be a fair statement, Doctor, that you cannot express an opinion as to the time of death in Mr. Harmandic's case, or this body that you claim to be Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say anything about the time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, in your report, which you have in front of you, under Tab -- at least in English, it's Tab A. It would be Tab C in your language. At the very end, under the "Opinion" -- do you find that yet, Doctor? You also indicate in that: "The state of post-mortem changes found as a result of a lengthy process which took place while the body was buried in the ground and may correspond to the time that elapsed from the moment the event occurred and to the description of the alleged events." My question to you, Doctor, is by your last answer, you do not agree with that opinion?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with this opinion, the opinion that we have offered here in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then would you tell me, what was the time and date of death?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to express any opinion as to the date and time, and the reason for it because I did not have all the elements to establish things that I would have been able to establish if I had a fresh body. That is, on the basis of bones alone, I can say that they were not older than ten years, which means that it's consistent with the period of when the war first started and the time of the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So in your best judgment, can you express an opinion as to the year of the date of the death, even?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the year is concerned and the time elapsed, you first have to ask yourself, where was this body buried, why skeletonisation ensued, why the body decomposed; whereas you have other bodies which were buried in -- at a similar time but they underwent the process of saponification, which means that they were in different conditions with a different type of humidity; whereas you had some bodies which were exposed to such conditions that the decomposition follows very quickly, that is, of the soft tissue and the internal organs, and so we are only left with the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You would agree with me, Doctor, that you cannot give or form any opinion and express that opinion as to the location of this body at the time of death, can you?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you an answer to that because I was personally present at the exhumation. I saw the structure of the soil. I saw the depth at which the body was interred, and I can say that the structure of the soil was such that it led to very quick decomposition of the soft tissues so that we were only left with skeletal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Doctor, let me try to rephrase the question. Perhaps you didn't understand. Do you have an opinion as to where the body was at the time of death, the location at the time of the death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand, Judge. Thank you very much, Doctor. I wish you a good trip back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, you were asked about the location and availability of a number of the articles that were found with or on the body; the bullet, the belt buckle, articles of clothing. Would an accused be able to make a request, either to your offices or to the local authorities, should they want to gain access to any of those items?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would first -- we would first have to check with the crime technical service of the cantonal police in Mostar. But everything else, all other articles are typically buried with the remains, unless the family specifically requests certain items which they would like to take home with them, in which case we allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were asked about the procedure, if you will, in terms of the family coming to view a body. And I wanted just to ask you again about that. Does the family decide what body they will view, or who has the authority to authorize a family to come look at a body, and under what conditions are such viewings approved?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the investigative magistrate and the public Prosecutor control the entire process of exhumation and autopsy, it is to them that we give the entire file, all the information, including the ones gathered by the crime technicians. And it is only after that that the family is allowed to enter the room where the remains are in order to view the body and identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But does that take place only after it's determined that the information provided by the family sufficiently matches the results of the examination, then, to justify taking that next step?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the investigating magistrate and the commission provide all the information, and then we add the information regarding the height, the age, and any specific features, we turn this all over to the Prosecutor. And on the basis of all this information and information received from the family, it is only after all that is gathered that the family members are allowed to enter the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were asked about the possibility of DNA testing in this case. And I should just simply ask you, was DNA testing a possibility? Were known DNA samples of Nenad Harmandic available to you such that you could have compared those with DNA from the body?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the autopsy, and after the completed autopsy, we turned over all the information and the identification was carried out and it was established that the deceased person was Nenad Harmandic. So that we did not take samples of bone for DNA analysis. In cases where the family says that this is -- this indeed are the remains of the person that they were looking for, then we don't take DNA samples for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the time of the identification, are you saying, then, that there was sufficient confidence that the identification was correct that it was felt unnecessary to proceed with the DNA testing?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, there was no doubt regarding the identification, and this is why the body was released to the family for burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, I would like to direct you to the letter opinion that was provided to you by my learned colleague Mr. Par during his cross-examination. This is the opinion of Dr. Josip Skavic. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wanted to compare this opinion and the methods used to those found in the examination and methods that you applied. First of all, it appeared to me that Dr. Skavic applied the same method in respect of calculations of body height based on the length of the femur and the length of the humerus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic used here, that is, he rounded off, as far as the femur is concerned; he put the figure of 185. That is correct, 185 is correct because the femur was 50 centimetres long. And if you calculate, as I stated previously, based on the tables, that the length of the body would be the length of the femur multiplied with 3.66 for males, which would translate into 185, even though Professor Skavic went a bit higher as far as the calculation is concerned. But that would be about 185.08.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking perhaps just a bit more general terms, the methodologies used. He relied in part on the length of the femur; you did the same something. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, however, it's beginning to sound to me as though the factor that has been used, based on the femur length, is perhaps different. You have been applying a factor of 3.66 whereas, as indicated in his letter, Dr. Skavic has used a factor of 3.76. And perhaps I should ask you whether that's a material difference or is a difference which can be reconciled with the factor that you've applied?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be reconciled with the factor because the deviation is not big in terms of the formula itself which is used for calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So in any event, do I understand correctly that in respect of the bone length, the femur, the humerus, that's a methodology which is consistent with the methodology used by you; so that you basically agree with each other on that point?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I have a table in front of me, and I said for males, the factor is 3.66 for the femur. And for females, 3.71. That is for females. And for males, 3.66.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I noticed that you applied an additional criterion based on the diameter of the skull, and that does not appear to have been considered by Dr. Skavic. And so my question to you, Doctor, is whether Dr. Skavic's failure to consider the diameter of the skull would affect his findings in any way, or whether it may, again, be something that could nevertheless result in consistency with your own findings?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: With skeletonised bodies, the number of factors used -- and in our case, we had a skull available, so this is something that has to be taken into account, because if you compare the proportions of the skull and compare it to the proportion of the body, the diameter of the skull in millimetres should be equivalent to the height of a person in centimetres. But because we had other bones available as well, we took both the femur and humerus in order -- and we took their diameters as well in order to get as accurate data. And if I looked at Doctor Skavic's report, he did not take -- he did not consider the diameter of the skull which we had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in your opinion, does his failure to make that calculation affect or, if you will, undermine his calculations in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an omission, because he should have entered that figure because, in any autopsy, we do that measurement, and that measurement is made part of any autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Mr. Stringer is going to continue this line of questioning, but I think that the witness did not answer the question. He did not answer as to how that would affect these calculations. But I am not sure if I have interrupted Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I could rephrase the question, Mr. President, or we could reread the last question to the witness. I thought the witness had answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may ask the last part of the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The failure to consider skull diameter, I take it from what you're saying, is a fairly standard factor which one would expect to find in an autopsy of this nature when one has the bones available. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you surprised that Dr. Skavic did not consider that or that he did not make that calculation in this opinion?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, he should have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: His failure to have considered skull diameter, does that undermine his ultimate findings in respect of body height?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sum of these measurements - the measurements of the skull, of the femur, of the humerus - would all provide a picture, and that would allow him to reach a conclusion which he would reach at the end of his finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, in any event, Dr. Skavic arrives at an assumed height of 185.08 centimetres. Now, would it be normally accepted that there would be some standard deviation plus or minus from that figure?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously I have stated that you can add 5 centimetres, that is add, plus 5 centimetres to the skeletonised bodies. And I have also seen in certain cases that more than 5 were added, but you can certainly add 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to take you to your statement that was provided to the Judges, on page 4, in which you stated that: "We determined the length of the skeleton to be 182 to 183 centimetres. This calculation has a margin of error of plus or minus 2 centimetres." Dr. Zujo, this is -- I'm taking this from -- if you like, I could put that document in front of you, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So first of all, now you've mentioned a deviation of 5, and you say you've seen a deviation that's even greater than 5. The deviation in your report is 2, so can we conclude from that that you were being a bit conservative in the estimate than that appears in your findings in respect of Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found during the autopsy that the diameter of the skull was 180; the thigh 50, and the other measurements. But as you say, we were critical, so we took 182 to 183 centimetres. Had we just taken the femur, which was 50 centimetres in length and the factor 3.66 for men - and I underline for males, and for women it is 3.71 - then that would be 185. If we were just to take the femur and added 5 more centimetres, that would make it 190, taking just the femur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now -- and in fact when we were talking about 182 to 183 centimetres, we're talking about the length -- I should say, we have yet to add an additional 5 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Which is what is done, then, to reach the height of the individual as a living person. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. When we added the head and the femur and the humerus -- for example, the humerus, 36, would correspond to 182; the femur, 185; the skull diameter, 180. So we took a mean value and said 182 to 183 in our report. That is an average. We didn't look at just one independent detail such as the skull diameter or the femur or the humerus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then by your calculations, that would bring the height of this person as a living human being to 187 to 188 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at all events, you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic having arrived at very close to 186 centimetres, so is it correct to say that, again, your final calculations are quite consistent with those of Dr. Skavic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please be quiet. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Stringer. Would you please re-ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, Dr. Skavic's figures come very close to 186 centimetres; his final calculation was 185.08. Yours come in, then -- yours come in, then, at 187 to 188. From a medical point of view, is the difference between your final number and Dr. Skavic's final number significant from, I guess, a medical or forensic perspective?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic just took 3.76 for the femur, and I took 3.66. Therefore, it's a negligible difference, or rather, not a very big one. He moved towards a female, because .71 is for females, and as I said, for men, it is 3.66.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you offer an opinion as to why Dr. Skavic applied the factor of 3.76?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection to all these questions with respect to the calculations of Mr. Skavic because this expert witness said that it was unacceptable because not everything was taken into account that he considered should have been. So if he does not accept it, he cannot, on the basis of Dr. Skavic's calculations, add, subtract centimetres and so on. I think it would be better for the witness to speak about his own findings as we don't have Mr. Skavic here. So that is the gist of my objection, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the last couple questions are quite good. You presented this report, and now it's the turn for this witness to comment on this report. But I don't think the last question is good because you asked this witness to offer an opinion as to why Dr. Skavic applied the factor of 3.76. I don't think it's a good question because this witness could only testify for himself rather than for another doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll try and ask it, perhaps, in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, can I just say something. From reading the reports of the Professor Skavic and Professor Zujo here, it is shouting out at me that both professors used different calculations because one professor used a calculation to work out the body of the skeleton, the height of the skeleton, to which he then added on 5 centimetres to bring him to his live height, and the other professor ignored the height of the skeleton and he only dealt with the live height. And obviously you have to come to different -- use different calculations. I mean, it's perfectly obvious from the reports that the professor from Zagreb doesn't attempt to arrive at a measurement of the skeleton, but he says that he is ascertaining what the height of the body is when he is living, the living person. And your expert here is dealing with a dead person -- I'm sorry, the skeleton, and then he adds on 5 centimetres. So the question really you have to direct to this professor, in my opinion, is that if he were to apply the same calculations, would they be valid calculations at estimating the live height of this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, you heard Judge Clark's comments. There have been two approaches taken; one is to calculate the size of the skeleton and then to add length to bring this to a living person. That was your approach. And Dr. Skavic's method was to go straight to the calculation resulting in the size of the living person. Are both methodologies equally acceptable in your profession, and if so, does that explain the different factors that were utilized by you and Dr. Skavic as applied to the length of femur?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the factors for the femur are concerned, I took the factor of 3.66 whereas Dr. Skavic took the factor of 3.76, .76. These parameters were found in literature. I haven't thought them up; they come from literature. They are tables that are recognised and contained in all textbooks for identification. However, this figure of 3.76, I don't quite know what it is because for females it is 3.71, should be .71, and for males 3.66. I applied the 3.66 formula. So on the basis of that formula, my calculations were that the length of the femur was approximately 100 -- or rather, the length or height of the body was 185 centimetres or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic uses a factor of 3.76, applies that to the length of the femur in order to determine the height of the -- the height of the body, the living body. You've done it differently, I believe. You've applied a factor of 3.66 to the length of the femur in order to calculate the length of the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the case if the individual is proportionately built. What do we mean when we say "proportionately"? It means that all the organs and bones are proportionately constructed, built. But we have, of course, individuals who are, from the waist up, higher, they are longer, compared to the femur and the legs. But that is precisely why we took these parameters. We took the head, we took the upper arm, we took the femur, and arrived at, if I can call it, a mean value for us to be able to determine the length of that particular body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The method that you applied is one that's used for a proportional body. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the method used by Dr. Skavic is one that would be used in the case of a disproportionate body?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he also used the same method just like the one we used, but he took a higher factor for the femur compared to our own factor which we recorded in the report, in the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's my understanding, then, that you are not -- you can't explain where his factor of 3.76 came from.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, Dr. Skavic also did not challenge your consideration of other aspects, such as the footwear, the clothing, other items found with or on the body at the time of the exhumation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although he says that the methods were not good ones. But I should like to know what the other options are if they are not clothes, height, age, and so on, what methods those would be. And of course, ultimately, the particle for DNA analysis. So all this is within the frameworks of identification. They are the basic input elements for us to be able to come up with something and tell the family members about the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You described, in your cross-examination, matter that remained around the bones, putrefied matter that was found around the bones of the body, together with articles of clothing, such as the remains of blue jeans. Are you able to say or give us an idea, any greater idea of the location of the 6.35 calibre bullet in relation to the jeans or any of the putrefied matter, specifically whether the bullet was inside or outside the trousers at the time of the examination?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body was wrapped in a military -- in an army blanket, and it was -- the body was lying on its back, which means that all the soft tissues were decayed and around the skeleton, so that we found the projectile in the region or at the level of the right upper leg, so in this putrefied matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The finding of this bullet, how significant was that in the greater -- among the other factors that led to the identification?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an indicator on the basis of what the family had told us, on the basis of what we found. So this was yet one more detail in the identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During my learned friend's cross-examination, you were asked a great deal about the height calculations and he on a couple of occasions asked you, I think, to speak to that issue in isolation. The identification process, is it one in which all of these factors are considered in isolation, or are they all put together?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those factors in the identification process are a conglomerate of details for us to be able to arrive at a conclusion that we can then tell the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the last paragraph of his opinion letter, Dr. Skavic states: "It ought to be stated that there is a number of elements in identification of the dead body of unknown person under the working number 05 which cast a serious doubt over the conclusion that it was the dead body of Nenad Harmandic and that all doubts could only be resolved by exhumation and application of the method of DNA identification." Dr. Skavic's opinion that these elements cast serious doubt over the identification, do you share that view, Dr. Zujo?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not share that view, the view expressed in the last paragraph because it is our task to assist the families, that we put all the pieces of the jigsaw puzzle together and that identification has taken place, and that is why we did not take particles for DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Dr. Zujo, your own opinion as to the quality of the identification of the body that has been identified as Nenad Harmandic? What is your own level of confidence in that identification?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that I have provided all the data and that the data has been set forth in the identification file for recognition and identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you confident that the body identified as that of Nenad Harmandic is, in fact, the body of Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The answer was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all the information and facts that I received, and according to the comparisons, what I compared, the information that I got from the family, I would say that everything goes to show that we are dealing with Nenad Harmandic when we compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that the last answer given by Dr. Zujo has been introduced into the transcript. I think what he said was, "I cannot answer that question."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear that part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, would you please make that clear for us. What's the answer of this witness to your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, they missed part of your answer. So I'll just simply reread my question to you and ask you to answer again. Are you confident that the body identified as that of Nenad Harmandic is in fact the body of Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: A moment ago, the answer that I got was that, based on the information and facts that you received, and according to the comparisons, the information you got from the family, you would say that everything goes to show that we are dealing with Nenad Harmandic when we compare the two.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But for me to claim that that is that corpse, on the basis of all the details that I was given by the family and the details that I found, that would correspond to the fact that the body was that of Nenad Harmandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Yes, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Doctor, from your evidence, as I understand it, your role was primarily to assist the families to identify their missing relatives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did your attendance at the interment place, the exhumation, and the autopsy have a dual role in that you were also investigating the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And would you say that the primary task which was being undertaken that day was to assist the relatives or to pursue a criminal investigation, or was it a bit of both? And I want you to think carefully about that, the criminal investigation element of the disinterment.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have understood your question. Exhumation and autopsy we conducted following an order from the court, the cantonal court in Mostar. That means that it was not the family which asked but it was the court which demanded an autopsy, and it was following the order from the court that we conducted the exhumation and autopsy process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do I understand from that that the order from the court related to a criminal investigation, and at the same time that that was going on, the commission for displaced persons took advantage of the exhumation to see if they could identify this person?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first was the court's business and the criminal proceedings. Now, the order of how the commission went and moved vis-a-vis the court, whether they had the information as to where that person was buried, I really don't know. I can't say. Because we were brought to the spot, to the Liska Park cemetery, we were shown the location, and that's where we started the exhumation. As to the details, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I'm labouring this, Doctor, but can we take it because you acted on foot of a court order that there was actually a criminal investigation being conducted? Is that a presumption we can make because of the court order and the presence of the police?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you were brought to that location, can you tell the Court, for our assistance, what was the -- what were the physical features of the ground? Was it ground on which grass was growing? Did it have any appearance of having been disturbed? Was it in pristine condition? What was the condition of the area from which this body was exhumed?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body was buried near a fence in the cemetery, and on that particular day, we conducted the exhumation of newborn babies who had died in hospital and we exhumed parts of bodies, and we were brought to the spot and shown where the exhumation was to be conducted. There was no soil. There was a sort of hole, I don't know the exact depth, but it means that some digging had been done there beforehand, and when we started digging further, we came across the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So are you saying, Doctor, that when you arrived there, that there had been some excavations already in the area of where this body was removed?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fresh ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was there grass over the site from which the body was removed?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just some leaves. At the bottom of this hole, there were some dry leaves. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was the body at any great depth under the soil?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not deep, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Were photographs taken of the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Everything was photographed. So if I understand you correctly, this body was removed untouched, insofar as you could, in its army blanket?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was it -- I think you said it was put into a special bag.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The digging up, when we dug up the earth, we came across a body wrapped in an army blanket. A photograph -- photographs were taken of the body. One photograph was taken with the blanket over it; another when we uncovered the body, under our supervision. And then the body, together with the blanket, was taken out. And when we had taken all this out, we photographed it again on the surface. And we then placed everything into the body bags. And on the bag was written the court number that we had, the date, and the number of the body itself. This was closed up, and the body was then transferred to the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: At what stage, Doctor, did you first become aware of the presence of a bullet? Was it at the site where the photographs were taken at the burial site, or was it in the autopsy room?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a precise answer to that question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think you said that you carried out this autopsy personally and your colleague kept notes. Would it be your custom to keep personal notes yourself?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we conduct exhumations, we create a schedule and we say I'll work in a room today, and he's, for instance, going to take all the notes, to draft a record. And I put on gloves and my smock and I am not able to really do the writing myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If -- I know you've conducted very many autopsies, Doctor, but can you actually remember this bullet?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot at this time, indeed. I, indeed, have done a lot of exhumations, but this one I just cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You're very frank. Thank you, Doctor. I would expect that after this remove and the number of autopsies. I know that you're not a ballistics expert, but the measurements which we have been given in the report of the 3.65 millimetres, I believe, bullet, are those your measurements or did you take them from a ballistics expert?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were our measurements. We have the instrument; and when we find a bullet, we measure it, and we say this is what it is. And the ballistics expert is the one who has the final word because he provides his own finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Because you're a forensic expert, obviously you've come across very many different types of projectiles, and I suppose you've become familiar with their sizes. Is there anything significant in the size of that particular bullet, 3.65? Do you know what kind of a firearm it would come from?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as firearms are concerned, I cannot say. But the calibre of the projectile I can talk about on the basis of measurements, but both the pistol and the automatic rifle used the same ammunition so I will never venture to say that this was fired from a pistol. I can say it is that calibre bullet, but if both a pistol and an automatic rifle are able to use the same ammunition, I am not going to venture and say which type of firearm it was fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I wouldn't ask you that. But can you say that the particular projectile that you found, the 3.65 bullet, was capable of being fired from a pistol?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, I've looked at the report, and it has been a subject of great debate in relation to your assessment of height and the alternative expert, the Defence expert's assessment of height. Do you see the point that I was making before is that if I take your figures where you arrive at 182 or 183 centimetres, plus or minus 2, which is the margin for error, plus a minimum of 5 centimetres - you said you've seen less -- greater additions than that - you say you arrive at an approximate height of the person when living, whereas the professor from Zagreb ignores the -- or appears to ignore the estimate of the skeleton and goes straight for the living height. So there's 5 centimetres between you on your maximum height and his average. If we accept that the information of 196 centimetres was absolutely accurate, even if you take away the diminution in height with the years which, in my assessment, is less than 1 centimetre between 30 and age 45, even if you look at that, you come down to 195 centimetres. Is a 5 to 10 centimetre disparity in height significant enough to reject an identification of this body as being that of a man who had a height of 196 centimetres when alive?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our finding where we say 182 to 183, and Professor Skavic said 185, and I provided my reasons, Professor Skavic took the femur, he took a different parameter for his calculation. Had I only taken the femur alone, I would have said 185. Even if I took 3.66 factor, that would have come up to 185. But 185 gives you another 5 centimetre margin, which is 190. But we were modest here. When I say "modest," we took an average. We took femur, humerus, and skull, and we came to a number of 182 to 183. I don't know where the figure 196 comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just suppose, Doctor, just suppose that in fact was an accurate figure. Just suppose for argument's sake he had been measured in the police academy the day before, and you come up with a maximum height of 190 centimetres, is the 5 centimetre difference significant enough to reject the identification?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I work on identifications practically on a daily basis, and I do it with a colleague who is also a forensic expert, and I can tell you that she allows up to 10 centimetres of margin. And she, herself, is a forensics expert. Her name is Eva Polinska. You may have even heard of her. We have worked together in Visoko. That is where the Tribunal has been working on some exhumations. The Tribunal has had an office there and they have been working out of that office for a while. But as I said, here I followed the literature to the letter. In fact, I have it with me. I can tell you that I am allowed a margin of 2 to 5 centimetres on the bone alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Doctor, my understanding of these charts, and my view is open to your expert opinion, is that the charts are a rule of thumb and not an exact science. But there must come a stage -- my question is, there must come a stage at which even in the area of inexact science, that an identification of a body must be rejected on the basis of height. What is the rule of thumb there? Is it 10 percent? Is the deviation from the findings, permitted deviation within what parameters before you reject? Obviously, if this man came in as being 1 metre 65, you would reject the identification as saying it's not scientifically possible for a man of 1 metre 90 to measure as a skeleton of 1 metre 65. So what I'm trying to find out is at height would this man have to be before you reject the identification on the basis of height alone?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put the question brilliantly. I work on identification every day. I have such cases that -- where you have documents, you find complete documentation on the body so the parameters are 100 percent accurate. But that would be drastically different. For instance, I found some cases where they had a metal plate in the femur, and I find that. And yet, the height does not agree with the height that I calculated, which means you have a deviation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So from all that, can we take it that height is only one factor that you consider but it can't be a concluding factor. Now, can I ask you about proportion. This man had the remains of a moccasin on one of his feet. And the size of the moccasin was visible, and it was size 45. Is that -- is there a rule of thumb in relation to the size of feet relative to height and length of femur? A rule of thumb, obviously not a science, a scientific exactitude.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my findings, I did not -- that is, I did not base it on the size of feet. His size is 45, which corresponds to tall persons, but on the basis of footwear alone, I never did that. I never estimated the height on that basis, except you can just estimate that it would be a taller person in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It has been pointed out to me, Doctor, that when I asked you about the relative or the relationship between feet size and height, and whether it was a rule of thumb or a matter of scientific exactitude, that you didn't in fact answer. I can infer what you are saying from your answer but it was pointed to me that you didn't say yes or no. Is it a rule of thumb or is it more scientific, the relationship between foot size and height?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no scientific principle of that kind at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you talked about the remnants or remains of clothes, the second expert's report refers to a letter or a statement which describes the fabric as being 10 centimetres long. Is that the extent of what you found on this body, just a little fragment of jeans?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Dr. Skavic wrote there, that it's a 10 centimetre fabric, I was surprised at this piece of information because we only said the remnants of blue jeans fabric, we did not give any measurements, so I don't know where this 10 centimetres comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, this is important, Doctor. I don't know if you can recall it but obviously there are photographs. When we are talking about fragments of clothes on this unfortunate skeleton, are we talking about a recognizable pair of trousers or just scraps of material?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what we found on the body, and we found remnants of blue jeans. In other words, this was the type of clothing that we found, and this was what was important for us. We found remnants of a pair of blue jeans. But I don't know how Dr. Skavic found this 10 centimetre patch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When the bullet was taken from the area of the body during the autopsy, would you follow the procedure of picking it up with a forceps and dropping it into a small evidence bag and sealing it until further examination?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We follow the principle that we don't use a forceps. What we -- we do it by hand in order not to damage the bullet. You can point at the bullet with forceps when you are taking a photograph. And we do that precisely because of the ballistics expertise that is to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Doctor, the reason I asked you that is because I understood you to say that there was material adhering, decomposing tissue adhering to this bullet, or that it was encapsulated.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that this decomposed tissue, the -- was around the bones, and that is where the bullet was, too. We did not need to use a scalpel. You could separate it with your bare hands, that is, with gloved hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The reason I ask you all that, Doctor, is I was wondering if it was possible that there might be some material for DNA available without having to exhume the body. That's the reason I asked you that. I was hoping that you were going to say that you removed some of the tissue with the scalpel, but you've answered otherwise; it came out quite freely.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: My final question is, did anybody consider or give you any information in relation to Mr. Harmandic's dental records? I shouldn't say Mr. Harmandic; the person on whose body you were carrying out the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the autopsy, we were unable to carry out identification of the upper jaw because of multiple fractures in it. But in the lower jaw, the right side, the three molars, and on the left side, teeth 3 to 8 were missing. But we were able to have an identification whereas we were unable to do so as regards the upper jaw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can you say that to me again. You were able to carry out -- did you compare your findings with records?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were unable to because the state of teeth in the upper jaw, both the left and right side, we were unable to carry out identification due to multiple fractures. But in the lower jaw, we were able to determine the state of the teeth on the left and right side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, the transcript here says we were able to have an identification of the lower jaw. So you were able to -- when I say "identification," that is to make comparison with known dental records. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: HAMZA ZUJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not because we had to have had his dental records in order to be able to compare but we were unable to access those records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's coming up to 4.00, and we are under strict time constraints, so I'll just confer for a moment with the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's almost 4.00. I'm afraid we have to keep this witness here for another day. Mr. Usher, would you please show the witness out of the room first. I have to remind you that tomorrow we only have a half day, and there's some other arrangements for this courtroom for the afternoon sitting. So we only sit until 1.00. We'll resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 3.59 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of January, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
